title: What is known about 1RB1LD_1LC0RD_0LA0RB_0LE1LF_1RF0LC_0RB---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LD_1LC0RD_0LA0RB_0LE1LF_1RF0LC_0RB---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.

Its tape is a word of four kinds of words, 10, 110, 1000 and 11000. Counting how often the head crosses each word shows a counter: each 110 is a digit of base 3 (three times as many crossings as the word on its left), each 10 or 1000 one of base 2 (half as many), and at the places where blocks of one kind meet the other the counts change by 5/2, 3/10 or 3/5. The left end grows by three cells each time the base-3 block at the left end overflows, which is why it grows at irregular times.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves no halt in the first 107 steps (native_decide); the C simulator finds no halt in the first 1011 steps.

What it does. A mixed-radix counter written in words: base-3 digits 110 and base-2 digits 10, 1000, with a busiest point in the middle of the tape from which the crossings fall by a factor 3 per digit to the left and 2 per digit to the right (measured in one stretch of 1.9·107 steps).

Why it is hard. The digits are not fixed in place: the junction factors 5/2, 3/10 and 3/5 show blocks of one base turning into the other, and no rule for that, nor for the moment of the next left extension, is known.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/tmrun.c runs 1011 steps without a halt; 262 cells visited (203 left of the start, 59 right), 115 ones at the end.

claims.title: The left end grows three cells at a time
claims.text: All 61 moments in the first 1011 steps when the head, in state C, reaches a new cell at the left end have the shape C>0 0^2 1 0 (1^2 0)^m V, with V made of 1 0, 1^2 0 and 0^3 1; each is followed within 12 steps by two more new cells. m is not monotone: it fell 14 times, the last time at step 35,830,421,385 (from 18 to 16).

claims.title: Irregular, roughly geometric growth
claims.text: The left end moved at steps 1.5·10<sup>9</sup>, 3.2·10<sup>9</sup>, 8.1·10<sup>9</sup>, 2.3·10<sup>10</sup>, 3.6·10<sup>10</sup>, 4.3·10<sup>10</sup> and 6.5·10<sup>10</sup>; the ratios range from 1.2 to 2.8. The width grows like the logarithm of the step count (236 cells at 10<sup>9</sup> steps, 262 at 10<sup>11</sup>).

claims.title: A mixed-radix counter of words
claims.text: Between the left extensions at steps 230,340,555 and 249,136,554, the head crosses the left edge of each word (as the tape stands at the start) rightwards: 3,645, 10,935, 32,805, 98,415 times for four consecutive 110 words (ratio 3.000), then 29,524 and 14,762 and 7,381 over the next binary words (ratio 1/2 per pair), then ×5/2 into the next 110 block, 18,455, 55,365, 166,095, 498,285 (ratio 3), then 149,485, 74,743, … and down by halves to 1 at the right end. The junction factors are 0.300, 2.500, 0.600 (to 3 decimals). So the tape counts in base 3 to the left and base 2 to the right of its busiest word; the left end grows when the base-3 block next to it overflows.

claims.title: The left prefix is a base-3 block
claims.text: In the stretch from step 3,083,613 to 3,258,424 the head turns at cells 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20 (from the left end) 25, 75, 225, 675, 2,025, 6,075 times: exactly three times as often per three cells.

claims.title: The rule, and the question itself
claims.text: Not known: how the junctions move (which turns digits of one base into the other), hence when the left end next grows, and whether the machine halts (it halts only in state F reading a 1).

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>11</sup> steps without stopping. Counting how often its head crosses each part of the tape shows a counter that counts in base 3 on one side and base 2 on the other; how the two bases trade places is not known. This page runs the real machine in your browser and lists what is known.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 262 cells visited.
Crossings per base-3 and per base-2 word.
The left end grows three cells at a time, 61 times so far.

sections.heading: A word with no visible rule
html:
Stop the simulator whenever the head reaches a new cell at the left end of the tape. It is then always in state C, and the tape reads C>0 0^2 1 0 (1^2 0)^m V: a run of m blocks 1^2 0, and then a long word V built from the three tokens 1 0, 1^2 0 and 0^3 1. Within twelve steps the head moves out two more cells and goes back right; three cells are added each time.

Unlike the counters of its neighbours in this group, the prefix does not simply grow: m went up and down 14 times in the first 1011 steps, and V changes along its whole length between extensions. The moments of the last seven extensions are 1.5, 3.2, 8.1, 23, 36, 43 and 65 billion steps. Their ratios range from 1.2 to 2.8, so this is not a binary counter.

sections.heading: Counting in two bases at once
html: Cut the tape into words of the form 1s followed by 0s. Four kinds occur: 10, 110, 1000 and 11000. Now run the machine from one extension of the left end to the next (19 million steps around step 2.3·108) and count how often the head crosses the left edge of each word, going right.

From the left end the counts are 0, 2, 12, 44, 142, 430, 1,294, 3,645, 10,935, 32,805, 98,415: each 110 word is crossed three times as often as the one before it. Then they halve over a few 10 and 1000 words (29,524, 14,762, 7,381), jump by 5/2, triple again over the next block of 110 words up to 498,285, and from there halve, with a few more jumps, down to 1 at the right end.

That is the visit pattern of a counter: a digit of base b is passed b times as rarely as the digit before it. Here the digits 110 have base 3 and the pairs of 10 / 1000 base 2, the busiest place is in the middle, and counting goes outwards in both directions. The left end grows by three cells when the base-3 block at the left end overflows.

What is missing is the rule at the junctions, where the counts change by 5/2, 3/10 or 3/5 rather than by a whole base: there the words of one kind become the other, which is why the extensions come at irregular times (ratios 1.2 to 2.8).

sections.heading: What is missing
html: No macro rule is known. A closed tape language from windows of up to 6 cells (and of 8 cells read from the other side) does not close, so not even the place of a possible halt (state F reading a 1) is pinned down. The next step is to find out what V encodes, for example by testing whether the tokens are digits in some base and the extensions are carries.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.053). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 236 cells (179 left of the start, 53 right), with a density of 1s of 0.436.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

family: mixed-radix word counter: ternary words 110, binary words 10 / 1000, slowly growing left prefix (rule not found)
summary: Open. No halt in 10^11 steps. The tape is a mixed-radix counter of words: between two left-end extensions the head crosses each 110 word three times as often as the word on its left and each binary word (10, 1000) half as often, with factors 5/2, 3/10, 3/5 at block junctions; the left end grows when its ternary block overflows. The rule for the junctions is not found.
